title: Swap a cultural word or gloss it
statement: Whether to replace an unfamiliar, culturally specific word in a traditional tale with a familiar one, or keep it and gloss it, is unsettled.
detail: Curriculum feedback on a Grade 3 lesson built on a West African folktale asked in one place for folktales to carry the customs of a people, and in another for the tale's culturally specific word to be replaced with a familiar one. The course team recommended keeping the word and glossing it, since the word belongs to the source and an unfamiliar concrete noun with a synonym in the sentence suits the word-solving routine the course must teach. It put the point to a ruling as a judgement call; a later course record implies every requested change was made, and nothing tested which choice serves readers.

evidence.quote: The document asks in one place for folktales to carry the customs of a people and in another to remove the culturally specific word. Our recommendation is keep-and-gloss (see the verdict table).
"gourd" is specific to the West African source
An unfamiliar concrete noun with an in-sentence synonym is the *ideal* case for the word-solving routine we are required to teach (D4.19), not a hazard to remove.
it is a judgement call, not a rule.
Make all the changes they have requested - no exceptions
